**Given:** A smooth manifold $M$ and skew coordinate arrays $\pi_x^{ij}$
with the bivector transition law in [F1].

[F1] [[def-general-poisson-bivector-and-bracket]]: on a chart,
$\{f,g\}_{\pi,x}=\pi_x^{ij}(\partial_i f)(\partial_j g)$, and under a
coordinate change $y=y(x)$,
$\pi_y^{ab}= (\partial_i y^a)(\partial_j y^b)\pi_x^{ij}$.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-differentials-of-smooth-maps]]: the differential of
a composite of smooth maps is the composite of their differentials; in
coordinates this is the ordinary Jacobian chain rule.

[F3] [[def-general-poisson-bivector-and-bracket]]: with
$\pi=\tfrac12\pi^{ij}\partial_i\wedge\partial_j$, the Schouten
self-bracket has local components $[\pi,\pi]_{SN}^{ijk}=2J^{ijk}$.



1.1 On an overlap, write $J^a_i=\partial y^a/\partial x^i$. By [F2], $\partial_{x^i}f=J^a_i\partial_{y^a}f$ and likewise for $g$. Then [F1] gives $$\pi_x^{ij}(\partial_{x^i}f)(\partial_{x^j}g) =\pi_x^{ij}J^a_iJ^b_j(\partial_{y^a}f)(\partial_{y^b}g) =\pi_y^{ab}(\partial_{y^a}f)(\partial_{y^b}g),$$ so the local bracket is independent of the chart. Skew-symmetry and real-bilinearity follow from $\pi^{ij}=-\pi^{ji}$ and the coordinate formula. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The coordinate product rule gives $\{f,gh\}_{\pi}=\pi^{ij}f_i(g_jh+gh_j) =\{f,g\}_{\pi}h+g\{f,h\}_{\pi}$. Skew-symmetry gives the derivation rule in the first entry as well. Hence the bracket is a biderivation. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 In a chart, expand the cyclic Jacobiator $\{f,\{g,h\}_{\pi}\}_{\pi}+\{g,\{h,f\}_{\pi}\}_{\pi} +\{h,\{f,g\}_{\pi}\}_{\pi}$. Its first-derivative terms are $J^{ijk}f_i g_j h_k$. The second-derivative terms cancel in pairs: the terms with $g_{\ell j}$ have coefficients $\pi^{i\ell}\pi^{jk}$ and $\pi^{k\ell}\pi^{ij}$, which cancel after interchanging $j,\ell$ in the second term and using skew-symmetry; the terms with $h_{\ell k}$ cancel after interchanging $\ell,k$; the terms with $f_{\ell i}$ cancel after interchanging $\ell,i$. Thus the displayed Jacobiator formula holds for all smooth $f,g,h$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If every $J^{ijk}$ vanishes, step 2.2 makes every local Jacobiator zero. Conversely, on a coordinate domain choose $f=x^i$, $g=x^j$, and $h=x^k$; step 2.2 then makes the Jacobiator exactly $J^{ijk}$, so Jacobi for all local functions forces every coefficient to vanish. The Jacobiator is formed from the chart-independent bracket of step 1.1, so this zero condition does not depend on the chosen chart. By [F3], the Schouten self-bracket vanishes exactly when these coefficients vanish, since $2$ is invertible over $\mathbb R$. This proves the claimed Poisson and Schouten criteria and justifies the bracket in [[def-general-poisson-bivector-and-bracket]]. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A commutative unital real algebra $A$, a coefficientwise
associative unital product $\star$ on $A\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$, and its first
coefficient $B_1$.

[F1] [[def-formal-associative-deformation-of-a-commutative-algebra]]:
$f\star g=fg+\hbar B_1(f,g)+\hbar^2B_2(f,g)+\cdots$, and $\star$ is
associative.

[F2] [[def-general-poisson-bivector-and-bracket]]: a real Poisson-algebra
bracket is bilinear, skew, Jacobi, and a derivation in each argument.



1.1 For any associative product, the commutator $[a,b]_\star=a\star b-b\star a$ satisfies the Jacobi identity. For example, expanding $[\,[f,g]_\star,k]_\star$ gives $[\,[f,g]_\star,k]_\star=(f\star g)\star k-(g\star f)\star k -k\star(f\star g)+k\star(g\star f)=fgk-gfk-kfg+kgf$, where associativity removes parentheses; adding the two cyclic rotations cancels each of the six ordered triple products. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Associativity also gives the exact derivation identity $[f,g\star k]_\star=[f,g]_\star\star k+g\star[f,k]_\star$: expanding both sides and reassociating the four triple products leaves the same expression. Comparing coefficients of $\hbar$ gives $\beta(f,gk)=\beta(f,g)k+g\beta(f,k)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Since $fg=gf$, the coefficient of $\hbar$ in $[f,g]_\star$ is exactly $\beta(f,g)$. The coefficient of $\hbar^2$ in the commutator Jacobi identity from step 1.1 is $\beta(\beta(f,g),k)+\beta(\beta(g,k),f)+\beta(\beta(k,f),g)=0$. Skew-symmetry of $\beta$ converts this to the Jacobi identity in [F2]. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By definition, $\beta$ is real-bilinear and skew-symmetric. The derivation rule in step 1.2 and skew-symmetry give the derivation rule in the first entry; step 2.1 gives Jacobi. These are exactly the Poisson-algebra axioms in [F2]. [given, F2, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A unital associative real algebra $A$, its multiplication
$m\in C^2(A,A)$, and the cochains, differential, and insertion bracket
defined in [F1].

[F1] [[def-hh-cochain-complex-and-gerstenhaber-bracket]]: a $p$-cochain
has shifted degree $p-1$; $\phi\circ\psi$ is the signed sum of all
insertions of $\psi$ into $\phi$,
$[\phi,\psi]_G=\phi\circ\psi-(-1)^{(p-1)(q-1)}\psi\circ\phi$, and
$\delta$ is the displayed Hochschild coboundary.



1.1 Write $\phi\circ_i\psi$ for insertion of a $q$-cochain into slot $i$ of a $p$-cochain, with slots numbered from $0$, so $\phi\circ\psi=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{i(q-1)}\phi\circ_i\psi$. In $(\phi\circ\psi)\circ\chi-\phi\circ(\psi\circ\chi)$, terms where $\chi$ is inserted into the block occupied by $\psi$ cancel. If that block starts at slot $i$ and $\chi$ is inserted into its local slot $s$, the first expression has coefficient $(-1)^{i(q-1)+(i+s)(r-1)}$, while the second has coefficient $(-1)^{i(q+r-2)+s(r-1)}$; these exponents agree. Every remaining term is a pair of insertions into distinct original slots of $\phi$. For original slots $i<j$, the coefficient with $\psi$ inserted first and $\chi$ second is $(-1)^{i(q-1)+(j+q-1)(r-1)}$; with the insertion order swapped it is $(-1)^{j(r-1)+i(q-1)}$. Their ratio is $(-1)^{(q-1)(r-1)}$. The same comparison for $j<i$ puts the earlier insertion first and gives that same ratio. Thus, with $|\psi|=q-1$ and $|\chi|=r-1$, $$\operatorname{as}(\phi,\psi,\chi) =(-1)^{|\psi||\chi|}\operatorname{as}(\phi,\chi,\psi), \qquad \operatorname{as}(u,v,w):=(u\circ v)\circ w-u\circ(v\circ w).$$ [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Since $m$ has shifted degree $1$, $$[m,m]_G(a,b,c)=2\bigl((ab)c-a(bc)\bigr)=0$$ by associativity of $A$. Thus $\partial=[m,-]_G$ has degree $+1$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The bracket is graded skew by its defining formula. Put $e_{uv}=(-1)^{|u||v|}$. Expanding the graded Jacobi identity, the difference between its right and left sides is $$\begin{aligned} &\operatorname{as}(\phi,\psi,\chi)-e_{\phi\psi}\operatorname{as}(\psi,\phi,\chi) +e_{\phi\psi}e_{\phi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\psi,\chi,\phi) -e_{\phi\psi}e_{\phi\chi}e_{\psi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\chi,\psi,\phi)\\ &\hspace{2em}{}+e_{\phi\chi}e_{\psi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\chi,\phi,\psi) -e_{\psi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\phi,\chi,\psi). \end{aligned}$$ Step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{as}(\phi,\psi,\chi)=e_{\psi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\phi,\chi,\psi)$, $\operatorname{as}(\psi,\phi,\chi)=e_{\phi\chi}\operatorname{as}(\psi,\chi,\phi)$, and $\operatorname{as}(\chi,\psi,\phi)=e_{\phi\psi}\operatorname{as}(\chi,\phi,\psi)$. Substitution cancels the six terms in three pairs, proving graded Jacobi. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Apply the graded Jacobi identity from step 2.1 with the first two entries equal to $m$. It gives $2\partial^2\phi=\bigl[\,[m,m]_G,\phi\bigr]_G=0$, so $\partial^2=0$ over $\mathbb R$. Applying the same identity with entries $m,\phi,\psi$ gives $\partial[\phi,\psi]_G=[\partial\phi,\psi]_G+ (-1)^{|\phi|}[\phi,\partial\psi]_G$. Hence these operations form a differential graded Lie algebra. [given, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

4.1 Substitute $m$ and $\phi$ into the insertion formula in [F1]. The two outer insertions give $\phi(a_1,\ldots,a_p)a_{p+1}$ and $(-1)^{p-1}a_1\phi(a_2,\ldots,a_{p+1})$. The internal insertions give $-(-1)^{p-1}\sum_{i=1}^{p}(-1)^{i-1} \phi(a_1,\ldots,a_{i-1},a_i a_{i+1},a_{i+2},\ldots,a_{p+1})$. Comparing this with the displayed formula for $\delta$ in [F1] gives $\partial\phi=(-1)^{p-1}\delta\phi$. Since $\partial^2=0$, this also proves $\delta^2=0$. [F1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If a normalized cochain is evaluated on a tuple containing $1$, every insertion term vanishes: the unit either enters the inner cochain, which is normalized, or remains an input of the outer one. In $\delta\phi$, the only potentially nonzero terms when $a_j=1$ are the two neighboring products (or the corresponding endpoint product and boundary term); they have identical cochain arguments and opposite signs, so cancel. Finally, finite compositions of local finite-order differential operators remain finite-order differential operators by the product and chain rules. Thus the normalized multidifferential cochains are closed under the differential and the bracket. [F1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A smooth manifold $M$, $A=C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, $n\geq2$, normalized
bidifferential cochains $B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1}$, and associativity of
$\star_{<n}$ through all powers below $\hbar^n$.

[A1] $n$ is an integer at least $2$; all coefficients and cochains are
over $\mathbb R$, so $2$ and $3$ are invertible.

[F1] [[def-formal-associative-deformation-of-a-commutative-algebra]]:
the coefficientwise product uses finite sums at each formal order and
associativity is equality of each coefficient.

[F2] [[def-hh-cochain-complex-and-gerstenhaber-bracket]]: the Hochschild
differential $\delta$, normalized multidifferential subcomplex, and
Gerstenhaber insertion bracket have the displayed formulas.

[F3] [[prop-hochschild-cochains-form-a-differential-graded-lie-algebra]]:
with $\partial=[m,-]_G$, the shifted cochains form a differential graded
Lie algebra and $\partial B_r=-\delta B_r$ for 2-cochains, while
$\partial O_n=\delta O_n$ for 3-cochains.



1.1 Let $m(f,g)=fg$ and $x=\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}\hbar^rB_r$, so $m+x$ is the truncated product. For arity-two cochains the insertion formula gives $\tfrac12[m+x,m+x]_G(f,g,h)=( (f\star_{<n}g)\star_{<n}h)- f\star_{<n}(g\star_{<n}h)$. Thus its coefficient at order $n$, where there is no $B_n$ term, is precisely the displayed $O_n$; all lower coefficients vanish by the assumed partial associativity. The same insertion formula gives $\tfrac12\sum_{i+j=n}[B_i,B_j]_G=\sum_{i+j=n}B_i\circ B_j=O_n$, because the bracket of two 2-cochains is symmetric. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 In the shifted Hochschild DGLA put $R=\partial x+\tfrac12[x,x]_G=\tfrac12[m+x,m+x]_G$; the last equality uses $[m,m]_G=0$. The DGLA identities give the Bianchi identity $$\partial R+[x,R]_G =\tfrac12\partial[x,x]_G+[x,\partial x]_G +\tfrac12[x,[x,x]_G]_G=0.$$ Indeed, the derivation rule and graded skew-symmetry make the first two terms cancel, and graded Jacobi gives $3[x,[x,x]_G]_G=0$, hence the last term vanishes over $\mathbb R$. By step 1.1, $R$ starts at order $\hbar^n$ with coefficient $O_n$, while $x$ starts at order $\hbar$; therefore the coefficient of $\hbar^n$ in the Bianchi identity is $\partial O_n=0$. [A1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 By [F3], $\partial$ on 3-cochains is $\delta$, so $\delta O_n=0$. Each summand of $O_n$ is a composition of normalized bidifferential cochains. An input equal to $1$ either makes the inner cochain vanish or remains a unit input of the outer cochain; composition also preserves finite differential order. Thus $O_n$ lies in the stated normalized multidifferential subcomplex. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 Add $\hbar^nB_n$ to the truncated product. The order-$n$ terms in its associator that are linear in $B_n$ are $$B_n(f,g)h+B_n(fg,h)-fB_n(g,h)-B_n(f,gh)=-(\delta B_n)(f,g,h).$$ No term quadratic in $B_n$, or involving $B_n$ and a positive-order coefficient, contributes at order $n$, since those terms have order at least $2n$ or $n+1$. Hence the new order-$n$ associator coefficient is $O_n-\delta B_n$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The lower associator coefficients already vanish. Therefore $\star_{<n}+\hbar^nB_n$ is associative modulo $\hbar^{n+1}$ exactly when $\delta B_n=O_n$. By step 2.2, $O_n$ is a cocycle in the normalized multidifferential complex; such a $B_n$ exists precisely when its cohomology class is zero. For $n=2$, the defining sum has only $(i,j)=(1,1)$, yielding $O_2=\tfrac12[B_1,B_1]_G$. This proves the finite-order criterion without asserting that later obstruction classes vanish. [F2, step 2.2, step 2.3, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A commutative real algebra $A=C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, two
differential star products on $A\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$, and a gauge map $T$ as in
[F1].

[F1] [[def-formal-star-product-on-a-poisson-manifold]]: the products are
associative, their coefficients are bidifferential, and they preserve the
unit.

[F2] [[def-formal-equivalence-of-star-products]]: $T=\operatorname{id}+
\sum_{r\geq1}\hbar^rD_r$, with differential coefficients vanishing on
$1$, and $f\star' g=T^{-1}(Tf\star Tg)$.

[F3] [[def-hh-cochain-complex-and-gerstenhaber-bracket]]: for a 1-cochain
$D$, $(\delta D)(f,g)=fD(g)-D(fg)+D(f)g$.

[F4] [[prop-hochschild-cochains-form-a-differential-graded-lie-algebra]]:
$\delta^2=0$, so the normalized multidifferential cocycles modulo
coboundaries define the stated Hochschild cohomology group.



1.1 The coefficient of $\hbar$ in associativity of $\star$ is $B_1(f,g)h+B_1(fg,h)-fB_1(g,h)-B_1(f,gh)=0$, which is $-(\delta B_1)(f,g,h)=0$. The same calculation applies to $\star'$, so both first coefficients are normalized 2-cocycles in the complex of [F4]. [given, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 Comparing coefficients of $\hbar$ in $TT^{-1}=\operatorname{id}$ gives $T^{-1}=\operatorname{id}-\hbar D_1+O(\hbar^2)$. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Expand the defining transformation from [F2] through first order: $$Tf\star Tg=fg+\hbar\bigl(D_1(f)g+fD_1(g)+B_1(f,g)\bigr) +O(\hbar^2).$$ Applying $T^{-1}$ subtracts $\hbar D_1(fg)$, hence $B_1'=B_1+fD_1(g)-D_1(fg)+D_1(f)g=B_1+\delta D_1$ by [F3]. [F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Since $A$ is commutative, $\delta D_1(f,g)=fD_1(g)-D_1(fg)+D_1(f)g$ equals $\delta D_1(g,f)$. Thus the skew parts of $B_1$ and $B_1'$ agree, and their difference is the coboundary $\delta D_1$. With step 1.1 this proves equality of their classes in the cohomology of [F4]. [given, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The coordinate bivector convention on $\mathbb R^3$, and the
first-order obstruction statement in [F3].

[F1] [[def-general-poisson-bivector-and-bracket]]: in coordinates,
$\{f,g\}_\pi=\pi^{ij}(\partial_i f)(\partial_j g)$.

[F2] [[prop-coordinate-jacobi-and-schouten-criterion-for-poisson-bivectors]]:
the bracket satisfies Jacobi exactly when the coordinate Jacobiator
coefficients vanish.

[F3] [[prop-first-order-star-commutator-is-a-poisson-bracket]]: the
first-order skew part of any unital associative formal deformation of a
commutative algebra is a Poisson-algebra bracket.



1.1 On $\mathbb R^3$ with coordinates $(x,y,z)$, take the smooth bivector $$\pi=x\,\partial_y\wedge\partial_z +y\,\partial_z\wedge\partial_x +xy\,\partial_x\wedge\partial_y.$$ By [F1], its coordinate brackets are $\{y,z\}_\pi=x$, $\{z,x\}_\pi=y$, and $\{x,y\}_\pi=xy$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Using the biderivation rule, its Jacobiator on these coordinate functions is $$\{\{x,y\}_\pi,z\}_\pi+\{\{y,z\}_\pi,x\}_\pi +\{\{z,x\}_\pi,y\}_\pi =\{xy,z\}_\pi+\{x,x\}_\pi+\{y,y\}_\pi =x^2-y^2.$$ At $(x,y,z)=(1,0,0)$ this is nonzero; by [F2], $\pi$ is not Poisson. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If a unital associative formal deformation had this first-order skew bracket, [F3] would force that bracket to satisfy Jacobi, contradicting step 2.1. Therefore this smooth bivector is not the first-order antisymmetric commutator of any such deformation, refuting the universal claim. [F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A constant real skew matrix $\Pi$, smooth functions on
$\mathbb R^d$, and the canonical symplectic plane when checking the sign
convention.

[F1] [[def-general-poisson-bivector-and-bracket]]: the bracket associated to
a bivector is $\Pi^{ij}(\partial_i f)(\partial_j g)$.

[F2] [[prop-coordinate-jacobi-and-schouten-criterion-for-poisson-bivectors]]:
the Jacobiator coefficients are $J^{ijk}=\Pi^{i\ell}\partial_\ell\Pi^{jk}
+\Pi^{j\ell}\partial_\ell\Pi^{ki}+\Pi^{k\ell}\partial_\ell\Pi^{ij}$.

[F3] [[def-formal-associative-deformation-of-a-commutative-algebra]]:
coefficientwise products of formal series use finite sums at each order.

[F4] [[def-formal-star-product-on-a-poisson-manifold]]: the unit is preserved,
each coefficient is bidifferential, and the first-order skew part equals the
chosen Poisson bracket.

[F5] [[def-hamiltonian-vector-field-and-hamiltonian-function]]:
$\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$.

[F6] [[def-poisson-bracket-on-a-symplectic-manifold]]:
$\{F,G\}=X_G(F)$ in the library convention.

[F7] [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]: a symplectic form is
closed and nondegenerate at each point.



1.1 Since $\Pi^{ij}$ is constant, every derivative in [F2] is zero, so its Jacobiator vanishes. Thus [F1] gives a Poisson bracket for every constant skew matrix, with no rank assumption. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 On $\mathbb R^{2n}$, $\omega=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$ is closed because $$d\omega=\sum_i d(dq^i\wedge dp_i)=\sum_i(d^2q^i\wedge dp_i-dq^i\wedge d^2p_i)=0.$$ For $X=\sum_i(a_i\partial_{q^i}+b_i\partial_{p_i})$, $\iota_X\omega=\sum_i(a_i\,dp_i-b_i\,dq^i)$; if this vanishes then every $a_i=b_i=0$, so it is pointwise nondegenerate and is symplectic by [F7]. Equating $\iota_{X_H}\omega$ with $dH=\sum_i(H_{q^i}\,dq^i+H_{p_i}\,dp_i)$, [F5] gives $X_H=\sum_i(H_{p_i}\partial_{q^i}-H_{q^i}\partial_{p_i})$. Therefore $X_G(F)=\sum_i(F_{q^i}G_{p_i}-F_{p_i}G_{q^i})$ by [F6], exactly the bracket of [F1] for $\Pi=\sum_i\partial_{q^i}\wedge\partial_{p_i}$. [given, F1, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

1.3 The zeroth exponential term is $fg$, so $B_0=m$. For $r\geq1$, expanding the formal exponential gives $$B_r(f,g)=\frac{1}{2^r r!}\sum_{i_1,j_1,\ldots,i_r,j_r} \Pi^{i_1j_1}\cdots\Pi^{i_rj_r} (\partial_{i_1}\cdots\partial_{i_r}f) (\partial_{j_1}\cdots\partial_{j_r}g).$$ Each coefficient is a finite bidifferential expression. If either input is $1$, every positive-order term vanishes, so the unit is preserved; the series is well-defined coefficientwise by [F3]. [given, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 On three independent tensor factors define $P_{ab}=\sum_{i,j}\Pi^{ij}\partial_{x_a^i}\otimes\partial_{x_b^j}$ for $1\leq a<b\leq3$, with each operator acting as the identity on the remaining factor, and define $\mu_3(f\otimes g\otimes h)=fgh$. These operators commute because they are sums of products of commuting partial derivatives with constant coefficients. The product rule says that differentiation of the first composite factor is $\partial^{(1)}+\partial^{(2)}$, so $$(f\star g)\star h= \mu_3 e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}(P_{13}+P_{23})} e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}P_{12}}(f\otimes g\otimes h),$$ while differentiating the second composite factor gives $$f\star(g\star h)= \mu_3 e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}(P_{12}+P_{13})} e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}P_{23}}(f\otimes g\otimes h).$$ For commuting operators $U,V$, the coefficient of $\hbar^n$ in $e^{\hbar U/2}e^{\hbar V/2}$ is $2^{-n}\sum_{r+s=n}U^rV^s/(r!s!)=2^{-n}(U+V)^n/n!$ by the binomial theorem. This is a finite identity at each order, so it applies coefficientwise to these formal exponentials. Commutativity of the three operators makes both expressions $\mu_3e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}(P_{12}+P_{13}+P_{23})} (f\otimes g\otimes h)$, proving associativity coefficientwise. [given, F3, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

3.1 The first coefficient is $B_1(f,g)=\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\Pi^{ij}f_i g_j$. Skew-symmetry of $\Pi$ gives $B_1(f,g)-B_1(g,f)=\sum_{i,j}\Pi^{ij}f_i g_j=\{f,g\}_\Pi$. Hence the product in this example satisfies the first-order normalization in [F4]. When $\Pi=0$, every $P_{ab}=0$ and the product is the ordinary commutative product; no rank or nondegeneracy assumption is needed. [F1, F4, step 1.3, algebra] ∎
